title: Reinforcement Learning & RLHF
blurb: Tests why preference learning differs from imitation, the RL vocabulary as it applies to an LLM, the three stages of RLHF, the Bradley-Terry loss, reward hacking and the KL penalty, how DPO removes the reward model, choosing beta, and how to check that preference tuning helped.

questions.prompt: What can preference training teach that imitation of demonstrations can't?
options: To prefer better responses over worse ones when several are plausible
To follow instructions at all, which a base model can't do
To produce one exact sequence of tokens for each prompt it is given in training
To learn new facts that were missing from its pretraining data
questions.explanation: SFT says "produce this exact sequence". RL says "produce something that scores well". Qualities like helpfulness are hard to demonstrate exhaustively but easy to judge. Following instructions is what SFT teaches first, and facts are the job of CPT or RAG.

questions.prompt: In RLHF's vocabulary, what is the policy?
options: The prompt so far, which the model acts on
The reward model, which scores each complete response after it is generated
The language model itself, its distribution over next tokens
The written guidelines that human annotators follow
questions.explanation: The policy is the agent's strategy from state to action, which for an LLM is the model. The reward model produces the reward. The prompt so far is the environment.

questions.prompt: Why are humans asked to compare two responses rather than write the ideal one?
options: Comparisons are the only data format that PPO can read.
People judge which of two is better reliably, even when neither is uniquely correct.
Writing ideal responses would leak the answers into the test set that is used later on.
Annotators are not allowed to write text, under most labelling contracts.
questions.explanation: There is often no canonical best answer, but comparing two is easy and consistent. That comparative judgement is what RLHF and DPO turn into a training signal.

questions.prompt: What does stage 1 of RLHF collect?
options: (instruction, response) pairs written by experts
One correct answer for each prompt, checked by two annotators
(prompt, chosen, rejected) triples
Scalar scores from 1 to 10 for each single response
questions.explanation: Annotators see a prompt and candidate completions and pick the one they prefer. No correct answer is collected, only a comparison. Instruction pairs are SFT data.

questions.prompt: What does the Bradley-Terry loss ask of the reward model?
options: A score of 1 for chosen responses and 0 for rejected ones.
The right ordering, chosen above rejected, at whatever values
Exact reward values that match the human ratings collected in stage 1.
Scores that sum to 1 across all the responses for each prompt.
questions.explanation: L = −log σ(r(chosen) − r(rejected)) is minimised by widening the gap. Only the order matters. That is why the worked example's scores were all negative yet still separated within each pair.

questions.prompt: A reward model scores the chosen response −8.839 and the rejected one −12.693. Under Bradley-Terry, what is P(chosen ≻ rejected)? Give three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The gap is −8.839 − (−12.693) = 3.854. σ(3.854) = 1 / (1 + e^−3.854) = 0.979. The scores being negative doesn't matter, only their difference does.

questions.prompt: Why does Procedure 35.1 warn against mixing preference data and SFT data in one dataset?
options: They train different things: one response per row, or a chosen and a rejected.
DPOTrainer can only read the first 1,000 rows of any mixed dataset it is given.
Mixing them makes the dataset too large to fit on one GPU at once.
SFT data would be scored by the reward model, which inflates every reward.
questions.explanation: The two formats have different schemas and serve different stages. Keep them in separate datasets.

questions.prompt: What is reward hacking?
options: The policy finds degenerate output the reward model over-scores, which people would rate as bad.
The reward model is retrained in secret on the policy's best outputs.
Someone edits the reward model's weights to raise its scores.
Annotators give high ratings to their favourite responses in exchange for payment, skewing the data.
questions.explanation: A reward model is a proxy for human judgement, and any proxy can be gamed if optimised hard enough. Think repeated flattering phrases or stacked superlatives. It is an optimisation failure, not an attack.

refLinks.label: §35.2.3 The KL Penalty: Why Reward Can’t Be Maximised Directly

questions.prompt: In the objective E[r] − β · KL(π_RL ‖ π_SFT), what does the KL term do?
options: It sets the learning rate for each PPO update based on the reward.
It measures how much the reward model disagrees with the human annotators.
It rewards the policy for producing responses longer than the SFT model's.
It penalises drift from the SFT model, keeping the policy near its starting point.
questions.explanation: KL measures how far the trained policy's distribution has moved from the frozen SFT reference, and the penalty grows with it. That limits how far the policy can chase the reward model's blind spots.

refLinks.label: §35.2.3 The KL Penalty: Why Reward Can’t Be Maximised Directly

questions.prompt: After DPO training, the policy's outputs look almost identical to the reference model's. What does Procedure 35.5 suggest?
options: Beta is too low, so the policy wandered off. Try 0.2 or 0.5.
The preference data is broken, so beta has no effect and can be left alone.
Beta is too high, so the leash is too tight. Try 0.05 or 0.02.
The learning rate is too low, so raise it to 1e-4, as for LoRA SFT runs.
questions.explanation: A policy that barely moves points to too much KL constraint. Lower beta loosens it. Degenerate, repetitive output is the sign of beta too low. Raising DPO's learning rate to SFT levels is the common mistake in Procedure 35.3.

questions.prompt: Over two tokens, the policy assigns probabilities p = (0.5, 0.5) and the reference q = (0.9, 0.1). Using KL(p ‖ q) = Σ p(x) ln(p(x) / q(x)), what is the KL in nats? Give three decimal places.

refLinks.label: §35.2.3 The KL Penalty: Why Reward Can’t Be Maximised Directly

questions.prompt: Which does DPO avoid, compared with PPO-based RLHF? Select all that apply.
options: A frozen reference model
Training and hosting a separate reward model
Sampling from the policy during training
An RL optimiser with many sensitive hyperparameters
questions.explanation: DPO is supervised learning on a static preference set. It still needs a frozen reference model: its loss compares policy and reference log-probabilities, and that is how the KL constraint is folded in.

refLinks.label: §35.2.4 DPO: Skipping the Reward Model and the RL Loop

questions.prompt: At step 0, the policy and reference are identical, so the DPO margin is 0. What is the loss, −log σ(0)? Give four decimal places.
questions.explanation: σ(0) = 0.5 and −log 0.5 = ln 2 = 0.6931. That is the loss when the policy has no preference at all, which is where the worked example started.

questions.prompt: With β = 0.1, a pair has chosen_term − rejected_term = 19.53. What is the DPO loss, −log σ(β × 19.53)? Give three decimal places.
questions.explanation: β × 19.53 = 1.953. σ(1.953) = 0.876, and −ln 0.876 = 0.133. That matches the worked example at step 10, when the margin had reached +19.53.

questions.prompt: What does a team give up by choosing DPO over classic RLHF?
options: The ability to train with LoRA, since DPO needs every weight to be updated
Any form of KL constraint, so DPO policies drift much further from the SFT model
Stable training, since DPO is far more sensitive to its hyperparameters than PPO
A reusable reward model, for best-of-N reranking, filtering or automated grading
questions.explanation: DPO produces only a tuned policy. The KL constraint is folded into its loss, it pairs with LoRA (Listing 35.4), and it is more stable than PPO, not less.

refLinks.label: §35.2.4 DPO: Skipping the Reward Model and the RL Loop

questions.prompt: What learning rate does Procedure 35.3 suggest for DPO?
options: Any rate, since DPO's closed-form loss makes the learning rate irrelevant
1e-4 or higher, the same as a LoRA SFT run, since both use supervised learning
5e-6 to 1e-5, well below a typical LoRA SFT rate
1e-2, since DPO's loss is small and needs larger steps to move the weights
questions.explanation: DPO is much more sensitive to learning rate than SFT. Starting at SFT's 1e-4 or more is the procedure's common mistake. Listing 35.4 uses 5e-6.

questions.prompt: Can preference tuning start straight from a base model that has never seen instruction data?
options: No. Preference tuning needs a model trained from scratch on preference data only.
No. RLHF and DPO need an SFT model to start from and to act as the frozen reference.
Yes. Preference tuning replaces SFT, so the base model is the ideal starting point.
Yes, but only with DPO. PPO needs SFT, while DPO works from any base model at all.
questions.explanation: Preference tuning is the stage after SFT, not a substitute. Both methods anchor to an SFT reference. Without it, the policy has nothing sensible to anchor its comparisons against.

questions.prompt: Reward-model scores keep rising during training, but an LLM judge rates the outputs as getting worse. What is happening?
options: Reward hacking. The policy is exploiting the reward model, not improving.
The alignment tax, which always shows up as rising rewards with falling quality.
The judge is biased, so its ratings should be ignored once rewards rise.
Normal progress. Judges always lag behind reward models by a few hundred steps.
questions.explanation: Check 3 in Procedure 35.6 names this pattern. Rising proxy scores with falling real quality is the signature of reward hacking. The alignment tax is a loss of general capability, measured on outside benchmarks.

questions.prompt: A DPO run gives a 62% win rate against the reference, with order swapped to control for position bias. A general benchmark drops 3 points. What does the chapter say about shipping it?
options: Ship it without further thought. A win rate over 50% is all that matters.
Never ship it. Any drop on a general benchmark means the tuning failed.
Retrain with beta set to zero, which removes the alignment tax completely.
The 3-point tax may be a fair trade, but it should be weighed knowingly.
questions.explanation: The chapter says preference tuning can degrade general capability, and that may still be worth it for a production assistant, but it must be measured. Beta near zero would remove the KL leash and invite reward hacking.

questions.prompt: The reward model's head is a linear layer from GPT-2's 768-dimensional hidden state to one score. How many parameters does it have?
questions.explanation: 768 weights plus 1 bias is 769, the "trainable 769-parameter linear head" in the worked example. The GPT-2 backbone is frozen.

questions.prompt: The reward model ranked all 8 of its 8 training pairs correctly. What does that show, and what doesn't it show?
options: It is a perfect reward model, ready to use for any preference task.
It fits those pairs. Generalising needs a held-out preference check.
It proves the model has learned real human values from eight examples.
It shows nothing, since rankings on training pairs are random by construction.
questions.explanation: Eight training pairs ranked correctly shows the loss did its job. Procedure 35.6 asks for a held-out sanity check before trusting a reward model. The chapter also warns reward models can pick up biases like length and style.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the RL vocabulary table, state what the "action" and "reward" are for an LLM being trained with RLHF, and explain in one sentence why the reward is typically assigned to a whole response rather than to each individual token.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: For an LLM trained with RLHF, the "action" is emitting the next token (or, at a coarser grain, the whole response), and the "reward" is a scalar score assigned to the full response by a reward model. The reward is assigned to the whole response rather than to each token because there is no reliable way to judge whether an individual token, in isolation, was "good." Quality (helpfulness, coherence, tone) is a property of the completed response, not of any single token in it. A token that looks poor in isolation might be a necessary step toward a strong overall answer.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain, in your own words, why the Bradley-Terry loss never demands a specific reward value, only that `r(chosen) > r(rejected)`. What would change about a reward model's outputs if the loss instead demanded a specific value for each score?
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The Bradley-Terry loss, $-\log \sigma(r(\text{chosen}) - r(\text{rejected}))$, is minimised as the *gap* between the two scores grows, regardless of where that gap sits on the number line. It never appears in a form that compares either score against a fixed target value. If the loss instead demanded a specific value per response (e.g. a mean-squared-error loss against hand-assigned scores of 1.0 and 0.0), the reward model would need genuinely calibrated absolute scores from annotators, which is a much harder and more expensive labelling task than a simple pairwise preference. And the model's outputs would no longer be free to occupy whatever numeric range best separates good from bad, the way the chapter's worked example showed both `chosen` and `rejected` scores landing in a shared negative range while still ranking correctly.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 35.1 as a template, write three new `(prompt, chosen, rejected)` triples for a domain of your choosing (not customer support or general trivia), following the pattern from the Worked Example where `chosen` is helpful and complete and `rejected` is terse or evasive.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only, no single answer. A representative example set for, say, a legal-summary domain: `chosen` responses that name the correct governing clause and cite it plainly, `rejected` responses that give a vague gist without citation, following the chapter's Worked Example pattern of complete-and-cited versus terse-and-unsupported.

bookExercises.prompt: The Worked Example's DPO run started with margin `+0.0000` at step 0 and reached `+40.72` by the final step. Using Listing 35.3's formula, explain algebraically why the margin must be exactly zero at step 0, before any training has occurred, regardless of which preference pairs are used.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: In Listing 35.3, at step 0 the policy and reference model are literally the same weights (the reference is initialised as a frozen copy of the starting policy). Therefore `sequence_logprob(policy, prompt, response)` and `sequence_logprob(reference, prompt, response)` return identical values for any response, so `chosen_term = logp_chosen_policy - logp_chosen_ref = 0` and `rejected_term = 0` as well, making `chosen_term - rejected_term = 0`. The margin is algebraically forced to zero regardless of which preference pairs are used, because no gradient step has yet moved the policy away from the reference.

bookExercises.prompt: A team preference-tuned a model with DPO and observed the reward-model-analogous preference margin rising steadily, but a human reviewer reports the model's outputs have become oddly repetitive. Using this chapter's Trade-offs and Procedure 35.5, name the likely cause and the specific hyperparameter change you'd try first.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The likely cause is `beta` set too low. The KL leash is too loose, so the policy has wandered far enough from the reference model to start exploiting the reward model's blind spots (reward hacking), which manifests as the repetitive text the reviewer noticed even as the (proxy) preference margin keeps climbing. The specific change to try first, per Procedure 35.5, is raising `beta` (e.g. from 0.1 to 0.2 or 0.5) to tighten the constraint back toward the reference model, then re-checking actual generations rather than the margin alone.

bookExercises.prompt: A customer wants to preference-tune a foundation model but has never run instruction fine-tuning on it. Using this chapter's "How This Connects" framing, explain in two or three sentences why you'd recommend against skipping straight to DPO.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Both PPO-based RLHF and DPO need an SFT model to serve two roles at once: the starting point for the policy being optimised, and the frozen reference model that anchors the KL penalty (explicit in PPO, folded into DPO's loss). Skipping SFT means preference-tuning would start from, and be anchored to, a base model that has never learned to follow instructions at all, so the "reference" behaviour being preserved is not a sensible baseline to preserve, and the preference pairs (which assume instruction-following completions) would be out of distribution for what the base model naturally produces.

bookExercises.prompt: Read the DPO paper's (Rafailov et al.) derivation of the closed-form relationship between the optimal policy and the reward function. Summarise, in your own words, the key algebraic step that lets the reward model be eliminated from the loss.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only, no single answer, since it requires reading the DPO paper. Expect an answer to identify that the key step is recognising the KL-constrained reward-maximisation objective has a known closed-form optimal policy (a Boltzmann-like distribution over the reward), which lets the reward function be expressed algebraically in terms of the optimal policy and the reference policy. Substituting that expression back into the Bradley-Terry loss cancels the explicit reward model out entirely, leaving a loss defined purely on the policy's own log-probabilities.

bookExercises.prompt: Compare the "alignment tax" mentioned in this chapter's Trade-offs section to the concept of overfitting from earlier in this book. Are they the same failure mode measured on different axes, or genuinely different phenomena? Justify your answer with reference to what each one trades away.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only, no single answer. Consider: overfitting is a mismatch between training-set performance and true generalisation, caused by fitting noise specific to the training data. The "alignment tax" is a measurable drop in a preference-tuned model's performance on *general* capability benchmarks it wasn't tuned on, relative to the SFT checkpoint it started from. They share the shape of "optimizing for one objective costs performance on another," but overfitting is about a model learning spurious training-specific patterns, while the alignment tax is about a model's capacity or behaviour genuinely shifting toward the preference-tuning objective (helpfulness, tone, safety) at some cost to unrelated capabilities. It's worth arguing whether that's better framed as a capacity trade-off than as noise-fitting.
